blocks.text: An {blue|inequality} compares two expressions instead of equating them. Where an equation usually pins down one value, an inequality's solutions form a **range** (in one variable) or a whole **region** (in two variables)—so the right mental picture is a shaded number line or a shaded half-plane, not a single point.
Strategies

items: **Solve like an equation—with one extra rule:** multiplying or dividing both sides by a *negative* flips the inequality sign.
**Translate words precisely.** “At least” and “at most” include equality ($\geq$, $\leq$); “more than” and “fewer than” do not ($>$, $<$).
**A point satisfies an inequality** if substituting gives a true statement; for a system it must satisfy **every** inequality.
**On graphs:** solid boundary for $\leq$ / $\geq$, dashed for $<$ / $>$; shade the side where a test point works.
**Sanity-check with an easy number** from your solution range—it takes five seconds and catches sign-flip errors.

blocks.text: Inequality answers are *sets*, so the question always narrows them somehow: “which inequality represents…,” “which point satisfies…,” or “what is the greatest/least value….” Spot which narrowing is being asked before you compute.
Use exactly the moves you know from equations—add, subtract, multiply, divide on both sides. The solution is a range, drawn on a number line with a circle and a ray.
Which values of $x$ satisfy $3x + 5 < 20$?

items.note: Divide both sides by $3$ (positive — no flip)

blocks.caption: $x < 5$: an **open** circle — $5$ itself is *not* a solution.
blocks.alt: Number line with an open circle at 5 and shading to the left

blocks.text: **Check** with an easy number from the range, like $x = 0$: $3(0) + 5 = 5 < 20$ {green|✓}
The Flip Rule

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a **negative number** reverses the inequality sign. (Adding or subtracting never flips it.)
Which values of $x$ satisfy $12 - 2x \geq 4$?

items.text: $-2x \geq -8 \;\Rightarrow\; x \leq 4$
items.note: Divided by $-2$ and flipped. Check $x = 0$: $12 - 0 \geq 4$ is true, and $0 \leq 4$ agrees.

items.text: $-2x \geq -8 \;\Rightarrow\; x \geq 4$
items.note: Divided by a negative without flipping. Check $x = 5$: $12 - 10 = 2 \geq 4$ is false — the range is wrong.

blocks.caption: $x \leq 4$: a **closed** circle — $4$ itself *is* a solution.
blocks.alt: Number line with a closed circle at 4 and shading to the left

blocks.text: You can dodge the flip entirely: from $12 - 2x \geq 4$, **add** $2x$ to both sides to get $12 \geq 4 + 2x$, then $8 \geq 2x$, so $4 \geq x$. Same answer, no negative division, no flip to forget.

Most SAT inequality questions are word problems about **limits**: budgets, capacities, minimum goals. The equation-building skeleton is the same as before—what's new is choosing the right symbol, and the strict/inclusive distinction does real work.
Amir has $\$60$ to spend at the movies. A ticket costs $\$14$, and snacks cost $\$8$ each. What is the greatest number of snacks he can buy?
“Has $\$60$ to spend” means the total can't exceed $60$—spending **at most** $\$60$:

items.note: Ticket plus $8$ per snack, capped at $60$

blocks.text: Snacks come in whole numbers, so the greatest value is $s = \green{5}$—**round down**, because $6$ snacks would cost $14 + 48 = \$62$, over budget. A fractional cutoff always rounds *toward* the allowed side.

blocks.stem: A freight elevator can carry **at most** $2{,}000$ pounds. The operator weighs $180$ pounds, and each crate weighs $65$ pounds. Which inequality gives all possible numbers of crates $c$ the elevator can carry with the operator aboard?

items.text: Total weight is $65$ per crate plus the operator's $180$, and “at most” allows equality: $\leq 2{,}000$. (In fact $c = 28$ hits $2{,}000$ exactly—and it's allowed.)
The strict $<$ wrongly forbids loading exactly $2{,}000$ pounds—but “at most $2{,}000$” includes $2{,}000$.
Flipped direction: this demands the elevator be loaded *to at least* its limit.
Grouping error: it multiplies the operator's weight by $65$ too. Only crates cost $65$ pounds each.

blocks.text: Strict vs. inclusive is a favorite trap: “at most” and “at least” **include** the boundary ($\leq$, $\geq$); “fewer than” and “more than” **exclude** it ($<$, $>$). One word changes the symbol.

A two-variable inequality like $y \leq x + 1$ is satisfied by every point on one **side** of a line. Its graph has two parts: the {blue|boundary line} $y = x + 1$, and the {teal|shaded half-plane} of solutions.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Boundary: **solid** for $\leq$ or $\geq$ (points on the line count), **dashed** for $<$ or $>$ (they don't). Solved for $y$: shade **above** for $y >$, **below** for $y <$.

blocks.caption: $(2, 1)$: $1 \leq 3$ {green|✓} — in. $(-1, 3)$: $3 \leq 0$ {rose|✗} — out.
blocks.alt: A solid line with the region below it shaded; one point inside and one outside

blocks.caption: Dashed boundary: points **on** the line are not solutions.
blocks.alt: A dashed line with the region above it shaded

blocks.text: The Test-Point Method

Not sure which side to shade—or which side a graph is shading? **Test one easy point.** The origin $(0, 0)$ is ideal whenever it's not on the boundary: for $y \leq x + 1$, testing gives $0 \leq 1$, true—so the solution side is the side containing the origin.

items.text: Is $(3, 5)$ a solution of $y < 3x - 2$?  Test: $5 < 3(3) - 2 = 7$
items.note: True — the point lies in the shaded region.

items.text: Is $(2, 5)$ a solution of $y < 3x - 2$?  Test: $5 < 3(2) - 2 = 4$
items.note: False — the point lies on the wrong side of the boundary.

blocks.text: On the SAT you rarely need to *draw* the region—testing the given points against the inequality is almost always faster than graphing.
A system of inequalities asks for points that satisfy **all** of its inequalities at once. Graphically, that's where the shaded regions **overlap**:

blocks.caption: The doubly-shaded wedge satisfies **both** inequalities; $(3, 2)$ is in it.
blocks.alt: Two overlapping shaded half-planes forming a wedge, with the point (3, 2) inside the overlap

blocks.stem: Which ordered pair $(x, y)$ satisfies the system above?

items.text: First: $2 \leq 3 + 3$ {green|✓} Second: $2 \geq -3 + 1$ {green|✓} — true in **both**.
Second holds ($4 \geq 1$), but the first fails: $4 \leq 0 + 3$ is false. One out of two is out.
First holds ($-3 \leq 1$), but the second fails: $-3 \geq 2 + 1$ is false. Same trap, other inequality.
The second holds ($8 \geq 4 + 1$), but the first fails badly: $8 \leq -4 + 3 = -1$ is false. One failed inequality disqualifies the pair—no matter how comfortably the other one passes.

blocks.text: Two Constraints in Context

Real-world systems pair a **goal** (“earn at least…”) with a **limit** (“work at most…”). Mara tutors for $\$25$ per hour and lifeguards for $\$12$ per hour. She wants to earn **at least** $\$300$ while working **at most** $20$ hours:

items.note: Works—and note that exactly $20$ hours is allowed, because $\leq$ includes the boundary.
Under the $\$300$ goal — fails the first inequality, so the pair fails the system.

blocks.text: Check candidates against **every** inequality, every time. Wrong answers on system questions almost always satisfy exactly one of the two.
Watch for the two classic traps as you work: a missed sign flip, and a boundary treated as strict when it isn't (or the reverse).

blocks.stem: Which of the following represents all solutions of $7 - 4x > 19$?

items.text: Divided by $-4$ without flipping. Check $x = 0$: $7 > 19$ is false, so the range containing $0$ can't be right.
Loses the negative: treats $-4x > 12$ as $4x > 12$ and then flips anyway—two errors trading places.
Loses the negative *and* skips the flip: solves $4x > 12$ directly.

blocks.stem: Jae has saved $\$140$ and saves an additional $\$35$ each week. He wants **more than** $\$450$ for a new laptop setup. Which inequality gives the numbers of weeks $w$ after which Jae will have more than $\$450$?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Total savings = starting $\$140$ plus $\$35$ per week—and “more than” is the strict $>$.

items.text: $140 + 35w > 450$. (Sanity check: $w = 9$ gives $140 + 315 = 455 > 450$ {green|✓}, while $w = 8$ gives $140 + 280 = 420$, still short.)
$\geq$ would allow hitting **exactly** $\$450$—but “more than $\$450$” excludes $450$ itself.
Swaps the roles: it saves $\$140$ per week starting from $\$35$.
Adds the starting $\$140$ to the goal instead of to Jae's savings—the $140$ helps him, it doesn't raise the target.

blocks.stem: Which ordered pair $(x, y)$ satisfies the system above?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Test each pair in **both** inequalities.

items.text: First: $1 \geq 2(1) - 3 = -1$ {green|✓} Second: $1 < 1 + 2 = 3$ {green|✓}
First holds ($3 \geq -3$), but the second fails: $3 < 0 + 2$ is false.
Second holds ($1 < 5$), but the first fails: $1 \geq 2(3) - 3 = 3$ is false.
First holds ($4 \geq 1$)—but $(2, 4)$ lands **exactly on** the boundary $y = x + 2$, and the strict $<$ excludes the line: $4 < 4$ is false.

blocks.stem: A robotics club has raised $\$96$ and sells raffle tickets for $\$4$ each. The club's goal is to have **at least** $\$200$. What is the minimum number of tickets the club must sell to reach its goal?

items.note: Current funds plus $4$ per ticket, goal included

items.text: $25$ tickets give $96 + 100 = 196 < 200$—just short. Rounding down only works for *maximum* questions.
$96 + 4(26) = 200$ exactly—and “at least $\$200$” **includes** $200$, so $26$ reaches the goal.
$50$ is $200 \div 4$: it ignores the $\$96$ already raised.
$104$ is the missing *dollar amount*—the subtraction result, never divided by the ticket price.

blocks.title: Things to Remember
items: Solve inequalities with equation moves, plus the **flip rule**: reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative. Adding and subtracting never flip.
Translate exactly: “at least” $\to \geq$, “at most” $\to \leq$, “more than” $\to >$, “fewer than” $\to <$. The boundary is included only by $\leq$ and $\geq$.
Whole-number contexts: round **down** for maximum questions, **up** for minimum ones—always toward the allowed side.
Two variables: solid boundary for $\leq/\geq$, dashed for $</>$; shade the side where a test point (try the origin) makes the inequality true.
Systems: a pair must satisfy **every** inequality; traps typically pass exactly one, or sit on a strict boundary.
Always end with a five-second check: plug one easy value from your answer back into the original inequality.
